description: We are a team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, working on the challenge “Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars.” Our team is interested in space, technology, data, and creative problem-solving. We are looking forward to collaborating, sharing ideas, and building an innovative solution together.
summary:
EarthTwin is an interactive web platform developed by Team PLANEX to identify and explore potential Earth analog locations for future lunar and Martian missions. It focuses on two mission scenarios: Artemis IV for the Moon and SkyFall for Mars.

EarthTwin addresses the challenge by comparing selected lunar and Martian target regions with locations on Earth using geographic visualization, NASA, USGS and ESA environmental and terrain data, and a multi-criteria similarity assessment. It presents ranked candidate locations and allows users to explore their similarities and differences, helping them understand why certain Earth environments may serve as relevant analogs.

Identifying suitable Earth analogs is important because they provide accessible environments for studying planetary conditions, testing equipment, evaluating operational challenges, and preparing for future space missions. By making these comparisons more accessible and data-informed, EarthTwin aims to support research, mission preparation, and a better understanding of the challenges of exploring the Moon and Mars.
details:
GitHub repository: https://github.com/es-ratt/earthtwin

WHAT IT DOES

EarthTwin helps mission planners and analog-testing teams find where on Earth best resembles the landing targets of NASA's upcoming Artemis IV (Moon, south pole) and SkyFall (Mars) missions. The user selects a mission and a target site, and EarthTwin ranks 18 Earth locations with a Similarity Score from 0 to 100 percent. It shows the top five analogs for each target, compares each one with the target feature by feature, and explains in plain language why every other site was rejected or ranked lower.

HOW IT WORKS

We compare the same variable, in the same unit, on the same grid, on both sides. Slope and roughness come from NASA LRO LOLA (Moon, 240 m) and the Mars MOLA-HRSC elevation model (Mars, 200 m), and the Earth elevation data (NASADEM or ESA Copernicus DEM) are resampled to the same grid. Temperature comes from NASA LRO Diviner and NASA MODIS. Ground ice comes from ESA Permafrost CCI, and rock type, soil and logistics come from Macrostrat, SoilGrids, OpenStreetMap and OurAirports. Hard filters remove sites that break a published NASA limit, such as the SkyFall slope limit of 15 degrees. The remaining sites are scored with Score = sum of weight x exp(-|Earth - target| / scale) over slope, roughness, temperature, ground ice, geology, light regime and access. The weights are set per mission and are shown in the app. If a feature has no data, the app shows "No data", lowers the confidence indicator and renormalises the weights openly. It never guesses. A sensitivity check shows whether the ranking holds when each weight changes by 10 percentage points. Every stored value carries its dataset, version, date, resolution, source link and a confidence level.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Choosing an analog site today is often slow, manual and based on tradition or appearance. EarthTwin makes the choice measurable, repeatable and auditable. It lets a team see why a site was chosen, why another was rejected, and how certain the result is. The intended impact is to help planners shortlist testing sites for landing, mobility, robotics and resource-use technology before launch, to point to less obvious sites beside the famous ones, and to make clear where an analog stops being reliable.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Python for the data pipeline, terrain processing (NumPy, rasterio, pyproj) and the scoring engine, with 55 automated tests. JavaScript (no framework or build step) and Leaflet for the interactive maps. The site is static, with scores precomputed offline, and is published on GitHub Pages. Data are read through the Microsoft Planetary Computer and public APIs. The repository also holds a larger application with a Data Center, built with FastAPI and SQLite. We used Claude (Anthropic) as the only AI tool, for code and documentation. No special hardware was needed beyond standard laptops.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

First, it explains every rejection with numbers, not only the winners. Second, it treats the Moon's permanently shadowed temperatures honestly: they cannot exist on Earth, so for Artemis IV we match relative cold, slope, roughness, light regime and ice presence instead of pretending to match 40 K. Third, the scoring is transparent and open to change: the weights, scales and rules are in a configuration file, and the app reports confidence and weight sensitivity. Fourth, the top results include less-known sites, such as Beacon Valley and Duvanny Yar, beside the famous analogs, and the validation view shows where well-known analogs such as Haughton Crater rank. The home page is a live solar system in which the Sun, Earth, Moon and Mars glow as the focus.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific honesty came first. Earth has no lunar gravity, no hard vacuum, no space radiation and no Mars atmosphere, and the app has a Limitations tab that says where each analog works and where it fails. We left rock cover and Earth thermal inertia empty, because no same-unit Earth dataset exists, and we marked missing values instead of filling them. We kept NASA and USGS sources apart from third-party sources, checked the coordinates of all Earth sites against several references, and made the results reproducible: re-running the pipeline gives the same scores. We also kept the app lightweight (a static site that runs in any browser) so that anyone can open it without installing anything.
